title: Ranking Is Not a Property: Tolerance Budget, Dispatch Boundaries, and the Admissible Frontier
abstract: A kernel speedup is a point sample presented as a property: it does not say which shapes the advantage survives on, which reference realization scored the pass, or how much tolerance budget that reference already spends. We price all three on a DGX Spark (GB10, sm_120) and report where the original continuous-surface hypothesis failed. With rho the reference's own consumption in multiples of the contract budget, fp32 conv2d is a two-class dispatch surface over the declared tuple, not a depth function: a winograd engine at rho 10.195 with 0.52% of elements over budget and bit-identical output under every precision flag, versus TF32 tensor-op engines at rho 251.69 with 78.2% over budget, cut by allow_tf32=False. Class labels repeat 34/34 within one process. The engine sets how much budget a candidate must clear but does not decide the verdict: on all 56 conv shapes passing and failing arms exist against one reference. Admission is therefore a class baseline plus a measured within-class threshold: a two-line arm-class rule scores 96.4286%, a declared-feature model matches it at AUC 0.974652, and inside the hand-fp32 stratum the ranking falls to AUC 0.7548 with clustered CI [0.537, 0.9231]. The gate itself is one slice of a family: recomputing admissible sets at tolerance 1e-2 moves the fastest admissible arm on 24 of 56 conv shapes while the engine-class partition is unchanged, admissible arms 128 -> 203 -> 293 -> 672 across four tolerances. The magnitude diagnostic compresses (Spearman 0.986 with the class) while admission stays measured. Deliverables: a dispatch map, an anchor-normalized diagnostic, and a slice atlas of the admissible frontier, each with its validity domain on one device and one library build.
